claims.text: A conventional low-alloy tempered steel can be engineered to exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Optimizing tempering parameters will induce impurity-driven embrittlement within a narrow temperature window.
The proposed conventional low-alloy or tempered steel is susceptible to impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Adjusting tempering temperature, duration, and cooling rate can enhance impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
The transition includes ductile behavior at low and/or high temperatures and brittle behavior in a narrow intermediate temperature window.
Phosphorus or sulfur can segregate locally to grain boundaries in the proposed steel.
Tailored tempering promotes impurity diffusion and segregation to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation reduces intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion causes a sharp decrease in ductility over a narrow temperature interval.
Outside the embrittlement interval, impurities are more homogeneously distributed or their embrittling effect is mitigated, restoring ductility.
The optimized tempered steel will retain high ductility outside the narrow embrittlement window.
The optimized tempered steel will exhibit a marked reduction in ductility and fracture toughness within the narrow embrittlement window.
Conventionally tempered steel processed using standard heat-treatment parameters does not exhibit a pronounced narrow embrittlement window.
The proposed transition is expected only in conventional low-alloy or tempered steels with inherent impurity-segregation behavior.
The proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition is not anticipated in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
The embrittlement temperature range and magnitude of ductility loss depend on impurity concentration and alloy sensitivity to segregation.
TEM or atom probe tomography can be used to assess grain-boundary impurity segregation in the tested samples.
